Abstract:

Places can be defined as spaces that are inclusive of certain lived experiences, involving a social dimension. They are molded with various types of interactions, and are shaped, imagined and reimagined through stories and the prevalent cultural narratives. These place stories, deeply rooted in myth and collective memory, when re-enacted through ritual practices, revitalize cultural traditions and generate symbolic processes of Placemaking, wherein urban spaces are continually transformed into meaningful sites of collective identity, participation, and lived cultural experience. This study examines ritual festivals as dynamic processes of urban spatial production within the interdisciplinary framework of Literary Urban Studies (LUS). Drawing on spatial theory developed by Henri Lefebvre and Michel de Certeau, this study conceptualizes the city not as a static backdrop but as a performative and narrative entity continuously shaped through embodied practices, with the festivals functioning as forms of urban narrativity. Engaging performance and spatial theory, the study analyzes festivals as liminal, performative processes that reorganize urban hierarchies, redistribute authority, and reshape patterns of movement and interaction. It further examines festivals as processes of creative placemaking, where participation, memory, and embodied experience produce meaningful urban spaces, while also conceptualizing them as forms of social infrastructure and mechanisms of urban resilience that sustain continuity and collective life through recurring practices. Focusing on Odisha&rsquos urban cultural performances, the study addresses a gap in Literary Urban Studies by foregrounding performative spatial practices and proposing a cyclical model of urban spatial production.
